articles.title: Port of Tallinn secures new loan to refinance existing bonds
articles.summary: AS Tallinna Sadam, the operator of the Port of Tallinn, has signed a €50 million loan agreement with Swedbank to refinance existing debt obligations. The Estonian port operator announced the agreement on October 26, 2026. The unsecured loan has a five-year maturity and carries an interest rate based on the...
articles.body: AS Tallinna Sadam, the operator of the Port of Tallinn, has signed a €50 million loan agreement with Swedbank to refinance existing debt obligations. The Estonian port operator announced the agreement on October 26, 2026. The unsecured loan has a five-year maturity and carries an interest rate based on the three-month Euribor plus an additional margin. According to the company, the full €50 million will be drawn on October 26, 2026. The loan will mature on October 26, 2031. Tallinna Sadam plans to use the proceeds to redeem existing bonds with a total value of €50.4 million on their scheduled redemption date. The transaction will therefore support the refinancing of existing financial obligations rather than fund new port infrastructure investments. Port of Tallinn updates debt financing Tallinna Sadam operates one of the largest cargo and passenger port complexes in the Baltic Sea region. In addition to its port activities, the group provides maritime services through several subsidiaries. OÜ TS Laevad operates ferry connections between mainland Estonia and the country’s largest islands. Meanwhile, OÜ TS Shipping charters the multifunctional vessel Botnica for icebreaking and offshore operations in Estonia and international markets. The group also holds a stake in AS Green Marine, which provides waste management services. The latest financing agreement allows Tallinna Sadam to address its upcoming bond redemption through a new five-year bank loan. However, the company has not disclosed the interest margin applied above the three-month Euribor or provided further details about the overall financing cost.

articles.body: Houthi Missile Strikes Saudi Oil Refinery Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 27, 2026 © Adobe Stock/GoAerials Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Tuesday they had hit Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery, the ⁠biggest in the kingdom, with a ballistic missile. The Houthis also said they had attacked Saudi military aircraft and repelled an advance by Saudi-backed forces near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, an important Red Sea shipping route. Intensifying hostilities between Yemen and Saudi Arabia have further disrupted oil supplies and heightened the risk of a wider regional conflict, eight months since the Iran war began. The Houthis' military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said the strike on the Ras Tanura refinery had caused a fire at the complex, which also includes a shipping terminal and is located on the Gulf, west of the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the strike. Ras Tanura, which has a capacity of 550,000 barrels per day, was shut for a period in the early months of the Iran war as a precautionary measure. Nearly all Saudi Arabia's oil exports flow through two main ports: Ras Tanura in the Gulf and Yanbu on the Red Sea, both of which the Houthis have attacked in the past. Bloomberg News cited a person familiar with the matter as saying Saudi Arabia had contained a fire near Ras Tanura's terminal. AIRSTRIKES The Houthis said they had attacked two military transport jets at Najran Airport and an airbase in Khamis Mushait. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of the attacks. On Tuesday afternoon, civil defence authorities briefly issued an air raid alert in the Saudi capital Riyadh. The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government said it had intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards Riyadh. The Houthis said they had repelled an advance by forces they described as Saudi-backed from the southern approaches to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces earlier this month pushed the Houthis out of coastal areas they had seized in September, loosening the group's grip on a vital Red Sea oil route. Houthi-affiliated Al Masirah TV reported Saudi strikes on the Yemeni city of Mocha. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation. The fighting has shattered a 2022 UN-brokered truce between the coalition and the Houthis, who control the Yemeni capital Sanaa. On Monday, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met Iranian officials in Tehran to try to reduce regional tensions. Parliament in Egypt, which has said it is considering joining the three countries in a mutual defence pact, authorised Egypt's military on Monday to help defend Saudi Arabia if asked. (Reuters)

October 27, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Mertframe Turkey may reach agreements to make acquisitions or further explore for hydrocarbons by the end of the year as part of its target to produce 1 million barrels of oil and natural gas a day, Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said on Tuesday. Speaking at the Turkey Energy Summit in Istanbul, Bayraktar said Turkey had a production capacity of 300,000 barrels of oil equivalent, adding that the current planning had this reaching 550,000 to 600,000 by 2028 Reaching the target would mean more than tripling Turkey's current output, and even the level planned for 2028 would leave it well short. Bayraktar's comments show Ankara is looking abroad, to Africa, Lebanon and elsewhere, to close the gap "There may be more news, good news by the end of the year. We may buy, acquire companies. We are making partnerships and will continue to do so. There may be new fields, new countries, it could be Africa. Therefore, we want to reach that 1 million barrel target with these," he said Turkey's state-owned upstream oil and gas company TPAO has signed agreements for offshore hydrocarbon exploration in Libya and Pakistan, and has bought a stake in Iraq's Kirkuk oilfield. Turkey also has an agreement for offshore exploration with Somalia and has been carrying out operations in that region Bayraktar said Turkey was also exploring possible electricity trade with Lebanon and that it was interested in hydrocarbon exploration there too "Turkey has become a country that can explore for natural gas, oil with its own ships. We have a very strong fleet. This is why we're now going to Lebanon ... We are interested in Lebanon's offshore ," he said He added that some European countries were offering to buy natural gas from Turkey after deciding to halt energy trade with Russia over its invasion of Ukraine, and said that Turkey could be an alternative route for Europe while becoming an energy centre of its own (Reuters)

articles.body: Oil Prices Fall Amidst Middle East Peace Talks Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 27, 2026 © Adobe Stock/vadish Oil futures fell on Tuesday as attention turned to Middle East peace talks, though prices remain near multi-month highs as the Houthi-Saudi Arabia conflict rages and the potential for fresh US-Israeli attacks hangs over the market. Brent crude futures were down $1.00, or 0.86%, at $114.81 a barrel by 1311 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate crude was down 78 cents, or 0.77%, at $100.98. Iranian Security Council chief Mohsen Rezaei on Tuesday met Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei a day after holding talks with representatives of Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan. State media said Khamenei had emphasised the importance of pursuing Iran's interests and maintaining its conditions for ending the war. The four countries agreed to continue talks with a view to strengthening cooperation in peace and security, Iranian state media said. Scope for peace has been dented, however, by renewed attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis on key oil producer Saudi Arabia. The Houthis said on Tuesday that they had struck Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery, the ⁠biggest in the kingdom, with a ballistic missile. October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by a Washington-based think tank that has tracked maritime security incidents worldwide since 2017. Swiss bank UBS said it expects Brent prices to stay elevated near $110 a barrel through to the end of the year, citing volatile Middle East supply and geopolitical uncertainty. It was previously forecasting $100 a barrel at the end of this year. Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has risen but the number of vessel attacks has increased, with risks likely to become more acute if US naval support wavers, UBS said. Brent prices surged to more than $117 a barrel last week for their highest since April, buoyed by a wave of Iranian attacks on tankers around the Strait of Hormuz. Brent touched $117 on Monday as well. "The impression now is that there is a significant risk premium in crude oil prices for the risk that the US/Israel will attack Iran in the coming weeks," said SEB analyst Bjarne Schieldrop. Investors were also looking for cues from a general election in Israel on Tuesday. "The outcome of today’s parliamentary elections in Israel could also be significant for further developments in the war with Iran, as Israeli Prime Minister (Benjamin) Netanyahu, if re-elected, might attempt to achieve regime change in Iran," Commerzbank analysts wrote. (Reuters)

October 27, 2026 © Adobe Stock/namning Most Gulf bourses ended higher on Tuesday as diplomatic efforts to de-escalate the Middle East conflict gathered pace, a day after Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani officials held talks in Tehran. It was the first high-level contact between Iran and the three allies, who signed a mutual defence pact in August, since the US-Israeli strikes on Iran triggered a war that spread to Saudi Arabia and Yemen. Saudi Arabia's benchmark index advanced 2.3%, led by a 2.8% jump in Al Rajhi Bank, while First Milling Company soared 9.9% after the flour miller reported a steep rise in quarterly profit. Oil behemoth Saudi Aramco ended 1.7% higher. Methanol Chemical Company finished 9.3% higher after reporting a narrower quarterly loss. Meanwhile, OPEC+ is likely to keep its December oil output targets unchanged on Sunday, three sources familiar with the matter told Reuters, in line with expectations that no further policy adjustments will come before next year. Regional tensions remained high. The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said on Tuesday it had intercepted and destroyed ballistic missiles and drones launched by the Houthis at two regions of Saudi Arabia. The Iran-aligned group later said it had attacked the Ras Tanura oil refinery, Saudi Arabia's largest, west of the Strait of Hormuz. Dubai's main index leapt 2%, buoyed by a 3.4% rise in blue-chip developer Emaar Properties. GCC stocks extended gains as geopolitical worries eased and regional diplomacy lifted sentiment. Shipping disruptions on key maritime routes remain a risk, though strong third-quarter earnings could provide further support, said Mahmoud Mashal, senior market analyst at VT Markets Dubai. Also in Dubai, DIP Holding, owner of the Dubai Investments Park real estate business, is seeking to raise up to $543 million in an initial public offering. It would be the UAE's first potential listing this year. In Abu Dhabi, the index added 1.1%, with Abu Dhabi Islamic Bank increasing 5.7%. Post-trading-hours, the sharia-compliant lender reported a marginal rise in third-quarter profit. Among other gainers, Aldar properties was up 1.6% on higher quarterly earnings. Qatar's index jumped 3.4%, its best session since April, with Gulf heavyweight Qatar National Bank up 3.1%. The index had hit a more than six-year low last week. Outside the Gulf, Egypt's blue-chip index closed 3.5% higher, as all its constituents were in positive territory. Egypt's parliament authorised President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Monday to use "all necessary measures" to help defend Saudi Arabia, raising the prospect of Cairo's direct involvement against the Houthis. Photo courtesy Port of Los Angeles A labor dispute involving port watchmen could disrupt operations at eight marine terminals in the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach as early as November 1, just weeks after the nation’s busiest container port complex reported record cargo volumes. The International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 has warned fellow maritime unions that its members may go on strike when the latest extension of their labor agreement expires on Sunday. In an October 23 letter, Local 26 President Luisa Gratz said the union has been engaged in unsuccessful contract negotiations with employers and the Pacific Maritime Association (PMA) since 2025. “Although PMA has recently requested Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service’s participation, and Local 26 agreed, nothing of value has resulted from the Union’s commitment to bargaining in good faith with our employers and PMA,” Gratz wrote. The union said it has been operating under a series of contract extensions since last year, with the latest set to expire November 1. The eight affected terminal locations are APM Terminals (APMT), Long Beach Container Terminal (LBCT), Total Terminals International (TTI), SSA at C-60, A-90, LB 206, Pacific Container Terminal (PCT), and OH 55. The strike threat comes at a particularly busy time for the Southern California ports. Los Angeles and Long Beach both set all-time monthly cargo records in September , handling a combined 2.04 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) as strong imports and shifting global trade patterns drove cargo through the complex. The record volumes capped an unusually extended peak shipping season that has stretched well into the fall. However, the National Retail Federation expects imports to slow as the holiday shipping rush winds down, forecasting volumes at major U.S. container ports to decline from 2.25 million TEUs in October to 2 million in November. Local 26 represents maritime security employees and watchmen responsible for security-related duties at marine terminals, including gate and cargo watch operations. Their labor agreement is separate from the broader coastwide contract covering ILWU longshore workers and marine clerks, which runs through 2028. The PMA was also at the center of the last major West Coast port labor dispute in 2023, when contentious negotiations with the ILWU led to work slowdowns and terminal shutdowns at several ports, including Los Angeles and Long Beach. That dispute ended with a six-year coastwide agreement covering approximately 22,000 workers at 29 West Coast ports. While the current dispute involves a smaller bargaining unit, it raises the possibility of wider disruptions if picket lines affect terminal access or other maritime workers decline to cross them. In her letter, Gratz appealed directly to other maritime unions for support. “This letter shall serve as a preliminary notice of a problem and visible labor dispute, which will affect your members,” she wrote. “We are asking for your support and labor solidarity in respect for Local 26 Watchmen on the identified Marine Terminals in Long Beach and Los Angeles Harbor.” The International Organization of Masters, Mates & Pilots (MM&P), which represents licensed deck officers aboard U.S.-flag vessels, said it would provide further guidance to members working at affected berths as the deadline approaches. The notice does not confirm that a strike will take place, and the extent of any potential disruption remains unclear. REUTERS/Francis Mascarenhas Global marine insurance premiums rose 5.5% to $42.6 billion in 2025, but increased competition, excess capacity and currency fluctuations continued to weigh on the market, according to a new report from the International Union of Marine Insurance (IUMI). The figures, published Tuesday in IUMI’s annual Stats Report , show premium growth across most major insurance lines, supported by expanding global fleets, higher vessel values and rising demand for war risk coverage. However, IUMI cautioned that much of the reported growth reflected the weaker U.S. dollar rather than an underlying strengthening of market conditions. Ocean hull insurance premiums increased 9.4% to $10.5 billion, driven by fleet expansion, higher ship values and additional war premiums. Even so, fleet growth continued to outpace premium growth, pointing to sustained competitive pressure on insurers. Marine cargo insurance remained the largest segment, with premiums rising 6.9% to $24.2 billion. Growth was supported by seaborne trade and changes in commodity and asset values, particularly in China, where exports of high-value technology, including AI-related equipment and semiconductors, helped drive demand. Offshore energy insurance premiums were virtually unchanged at $4.82 billion, an increase of just 0.1%. London retained its dominant position with a 62.7% market share, including a growing renewables component. “The 2025 marine insurance market recorded modest growth in global premiums, although underlying conditions remained soft,” said IUMI Secretary General Lars Lange. “Increased capacity, competitive pressures and currency movements, particularly the weakness of the US dollar, all influenced reported premium levels.” Claims activity remained relatively stable during 2025, with no single catastrophic event significantly affecting an individual insurance sector. However, the accumulation of smaller claims continued to pressure profitability. Looking ahead, IUMI warned that geopolitical tensions are playing an increasingly important role in marine insurance markets in 2026, particularly as the conflict in the Middle East disrupts shipping and increases demand for war risk coverage. War insurance has become increasingly prominent as attacks on commercial shipping continue, while the availability of energy carriers has tightened amid heightened security risks in the region. “Looking ahead, geopolitical tensions continued to shape the market into 2026,” Lange said. “War cover became increasingly prominent while vessel availability, particularly for energy carriers, tightened as conflict in the Middle East intensified.” Despite concerns that tariffs would significantly constrain international trade, IUMI said the impact had been less severe than initially anticipated, while global economic growth exceeded expectations. Asia continued to lead growth in the marine insurance market, with China remaining the region’s largest contributor. European markets also expanded, although at a slower pace. The report also updates IUMI’s Major Claims Database, which now includes approximately 7,200 cargo claims representing a cumulative $11.4 billion in losses. Thirty national insurance associations contribute to the database, which tracks claims dating back to 2013. IUMI also introduced a revised Hull Inflation Index designed to help insurers assess rising vessel repair costs using broader economic indicators. articles.title: Hanwha General Insurance, CYTUR to Explore Maritime Cyber Insurance Initiatives
articles.summary: Hanwha General Insurance Co., Ltd. signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with CYTUR Inc., a company specializing in maritime and vessel cybersecurity, on October 23 to jointly pursue maritime cyber insurance business initiatives. The agreement…
articles.body: Hanwha General Insurance, CYTUR to Explore Maritime Cyber Insurance Initiatives Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 27, 2026 © Hanwha General Insurance Co. Hanwha General Insurance Co., Ltd. signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with CYTUR Inc., a company specializing in maritime and vessel cybersecurity, on October 23 to jointly pursue maritime cyber insurance business initiatives. The agreement aims to provide an integrated service combining maritime cyber insurance capabilities with vessel cybersecurity technologies and to actively develop South Korea's maritime cyber insurance market. As cyber threats targeting maritime supply chains, including attacks on vessel operational technology (OT) systems and disruptions to satellite communications, become a reality, cyber resilience regulations set by the International Maritime Organization (IMO) and the International Association of Classification Societies (IACS) are being strengthened. However, existing vessel insurance policies exclude general cyber-related losses from coverage, leaving shipping companies with significant gaps in coverage. Under the MOU, the two companies have agreed to jointly pursue Planning of maritime cyber insurance products and services Establishment of cyber threat assessment and cyber resilience-linked systems Establishment of a cooperative framework for insurance incident investigations (digital forensics) Research into scenario-based loss models. Specifically, CYTUR will assess vessel security levels and provide the technical analysis data required for insurance underwriting, based on its IT/OT cybersecurity technologies covering the entire vessel lifecycle, from design and construction to operation. Even after insurance enrollment, CYTUR plans to continuously monitor vessel security status through its cyber resilience management system and support risk mitigation and reassessments for insurance renewal. In the event of a cyber incident, CYTUR will analyze the cause of the incident and the extent of damage through remote analysis and onboard forensic investigations, and provide technical reports required for insurance incident investigations. Hanwha General Insurance will develop tailored cyber insurance products reflecting the characteristics of the maritime industry and oversee their operation. In particular, the company plans to establish criteria linking vessel security assessment results to insurance eligibility conditions and preferential measures. In the event of a cyber incident, Hanwha General Insurance will operate prompt incident reporting and loss adjustment procedures, and directly establish a cooperative investigation framework, including forensic investigations. The two companies will launch a pilot project and joint marketing activities targeting domestic shipping companies and shipowners in December. They also plan to develop policy-related cooperation initiatives with local governments and classification societies.

articles.summary: Swedish shipping group Stena AB has agreed to acquire Norwegian ferry operator Color Line, bringing together two of Scandinavia’s largest ferry companies in a deal that would significantly expand Stena’s...

Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Tommy Alven/Shutterstock Swedish shipping group Stena AB has agreed to acquire Norwegian ferry operator Color Line, bringing together two of Scandinavia’s largest ferry companies in a deal that would significantly expand Stena’s presence in the European passenger and freight markets. The acquisition, announced Monday , is subject to regulatory approval and is expected to close in late first quarter or during the second quarter of 2027. Financial terms were not disclosed. Under the agreement, Stena AB’s subsidiary Stena Rederi AB will acquire all shares in Color Group AS from ONS Invest II AS, which is owned by Norwegian industrialist Olav Nils Sunde and his family. The transaction would bring Color Line’s five-vessel fleet and four international ferry routes under the same ownership as Stena Line, one of Europe’s largest ferry operators, with 40 ships operating across 19 routes in Northern Europe and the Mediterranean. Color Line operates services connecting Norway with Germany, Denmark and Sweden, including the Oslo–Kiel route served by its large cruise ferries Color Magic and Color Fantasy . Its other services connect Kristiansand and Larvik with Hirtshals, Denmark, and Sandefjord with Strömstad, Sweden. In 2025, Color Line carried nearly 3.6 million passengers and 150,000 freight units, generating revenue of more than NOK 6.7 billion ($700 million approximately). Stena Line, meanwhile, operates approximately 35,000 sailings annually, carrying passengers and freight across an extensive European network. The company reported revenue of SEK 20.2 billion and employs approximately 8,750 people. The combination would strengthen Stena’s position in Scandinavian ferry transport while adding Color Line’s established Norwegian operations to its broader European network. “This is a true milestone in Stena Line’s history,” said Niclas Mårtensson, CEO of Stena Line, describing the acquisition as an opportunity to expand the companies’ operations and contribute to tourism and more sustainable shipping. Despite the change in ownership, Stena said it intends to preserve Color Line as a separate business, retaining its existing brand, Norwegian management and Norwegian-registered fleet. The Swedish group also plans to support further investment in fleet decarbonization, technology, digitalization, customer service and freight logistics. Color Line CEO Trond Kleivdal welcomed the agreement, saying Stena’s ownership would provide a stronger foundation for the Norwegian operator’s future development while preserving its established market position. The companies said there would be no immediate changes to ferry schedules, bookings or existing customer and supplier relationships. Both operators will continue running independently while the transaction undergoes regulatory review. articles.title: Japanese consortium plans ammonia supply chain and car carrier fleet
articles.summary: Seven Japanese companies have agreed to develop an integrated ammonia fuel supply chain and introduce four ammonia-fuelled car carriers. The project brings together Imabari Shipbuilding, Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha (“K” Line), Kyokuyo Shipyard, JERA, Shin Kurushima Dockyard, Nippon Yusen Kabushiki Kaisha (NYK) and Nihon...
articles.body: Seven Japanese companies have agreed to develop an integrated ammonia fuel supply chain and introduce four ammonia-fuelled car carriers. The project brings together Imabari Shipbuilding, Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha (“K” Line), Kyokuyo Shipyard, JERA, Shin Kurushima Dockyard, Nippon Yusen Kabushiki Kaisha (NYK) and Nihon Shipyard. The partners described the initiative as the world’s first commercial project to integrate green ammonia procurement, loading infrastructure, ship-to-ship bunkering and vessel operations. Chubu region to become ammonia supply hub The project will use Japan’s Chubu region as its central hub. JERA will procure green ammonia from markets including India and develop new loading facilities at the ammonia terminal next to the Hekinan Thermal Power Station. The infrastructure will supply a dedicated ammonia bunkering vessel. Kyokuyo Shipyard will design and build the vessel, which is scheduled for completion in 2030. NYK or one of its wholly owned subsidiaries will own and operate the bunkering vessel. “K” Line and NYK will also establish an equally owned joint venture. The new company will sell and supply ammonia fuel through ship-to-ship bunkering, primarily at the ports of Nagoya and Mikawa. Four ammonia-fuelled car carriers “K” Line and NYK will each introduce two ammonia-fuelled car carriers. All four vessels are scheduled for completion in 2030. The ships are expected to transport finished vehicles for customers including Toyota Motor Corporation. According to the partners, they will be Japan’s first ammonia-fuelled car carriers. Each vessel will feature a dual-fuel engine capable of using ammonia. The ships will also have enough ammonia storage capacity to complete trans-Pacific voyages using the fuel alone. Shin Kurushima Dockyard will lead the basic design work. It will then work with Imabari Shipbuilding and Nihon Shipyard on the detailed design and construction of the vessels. Safety measures for ammonia operations Ammonia produces no carbon dioxide when combusted. However, its toxicity and corrosive properties require dedicated safety systems. The car carriers will therefore include several layers of protection. These will cover leak prevention, detection and ammonia neutralisation. The bunkering vessel will also feature specialised equipment designed to prevent leaks and support the safe transfer of ammonia fuel. Through the project, the companies aim to establish a stable ammonia supply system for international shipping. They also intend to support the development of a wider low-carbon ammonia market.

Photo courtesy Hanwha Philly Shipyard Hanwha Defense USA is moving to take control of Hanwha Philly Shipyard, bringing the Philadelphia facility under its U.S. defense business as the South Korean conglomerate pushes to expand into American naval shipbuilding. The company announced Tuesday that it will acquire a controlling 60% stake in the shipyard through an HDUSA-led joint venture, a restructuring intended to align Hanwha’s commercial and government shipbuilding operations under a single leadership structure. The move does not represent a new acquisition by Hanwha Group, which purchased the former Philly Shipyard for $100 million in December 2024. Instead, it transfers control from Hanwha Systems, which currently holds 60% of the shipyard, to Hanwha Defense USA Shipbuilding LLC, a joint venture between HDUSA and Hanwha FutureProof. Hanwha Ocean will retain its 40% stake. According to a September regulatory filing in South Korea, the transaction is valued at approximately $237.6 million, with completion planned for October 31. Retired Rear Adm. Tom Anderson, president of U.S. shipbuilding at HDUSA, will oversee the company’s American shipbuilding operations. “As Hanwha Defense USA continues to grow its multi-domain presence across the U.S., bringing the Philly Shipyard under HDUSA will further align our government and commercial shipbuilding efforts,” said Michael Coulter, president and CEO of Hanwha Defense USA. “We look forward to continuing to invest in our Philly Shipyard facilities and workforce in preparation for exciting work ahead.” The restructuring is the latest step in a transformation that began years before Hanwha acquired the yard. In 2019, Philly Shipyard faced an uncertain future after delivering the last of two containerships to Matson, leaving its commercial newbuilding orderbook empty. With no new construction contracts, the shipyard’s workforce had fallen from approximately 1,200 employees at the beginning of 2018 to just 80 by July 2019. The yard turned to government work to survive, adopting what was then described as a strategy to “go gray.” Its first contracts involved maintenance and repair work on the Maritime Administration’s Ready Reserve Force ships FSS Antares and FSS Pollux , allowing it to recall some laid-off workers and put its drydocks back to use. Those early contracts helped bridge the gap, but the real turning point came in April 2020, when Philly Shipyard was selected to construct the first two National Security Multi-Mission Vessels (NSMVs) under a $630 million contract managed by TOTE Services. The program eventually expanded to five ships, providing the long-term production backlog needed to rebuild the workforce. The yard continued pursuing government repair work, including a 2021 contract for the Military Sealift Command’s USNS Charlton . Now, seven years after that initial shift toward government work, Hanwha is preparing to take the next step, positioning the facility to build vessels directly for the U.S. Navy. In August 2025, Hanwha announced plans to invest $5 billion in the shipyard , including additional dry docks, expanded waterfront facilities and modernized production capabilities. The long-term goal is to increase annual production capacity to as many as 20 vessels. Hanwha said in September that the shipyard’s workforce had more than doubled since its acquisition, reaching nearly 2,500 employees. The yard now has a substantial commercial orderbook, including three LNG-powered containerships for Matson, two LNG carriers for Hanwha Shipping and four firm medium-range tanker orders, with options for six additional vessels. It has also delivered four of five NSMVs for MARAD, with the fifth scheduled for delivery in 2027. More recently, Hanwha secured another federal shipbuilding program. Earlier this month, TOTE Services finalized a contract with MARAD to manage construction of the first of a new generation of Missile Range Instrumentation Vessels for the U.S. Missile Defense Agency, awarding the shipbuilding subcontract to Hanwha Philly Shipyard. The first vessel, Golden Defender , is scheduled for delivery in 2030. The program builds on the existing NSMV production line, with the new missile-tracking vessels sharing approximately 70% design commonality with the training ships. While that contract represents another step into defense-related shipbuilding, Hanwha’s larger ambition is to establish Philadelphia as a shipyard capable of constructing vessels directly for the U.S. Navy. That effort received high-level attention in September when Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao toured the facility and met with Hanwha executives to discuss shipbuilding capacity, workforce development and future Navy requirements. “Over the past two years Hanwha has made significant investments in the Philly Shipyard to contribute to the revitalization of the U.S. shipbuilding industry,” Anderson said. “Now we are positioning the shipyard to transition to dual-use, aligning shipyard operations, workforce, and customer relations in preparation to build for the U.S. Navy, other federal agencies, and commercial customers.” For a shipyard that was struggling to find work just seven years ago, the announcement marks another milestone in its transformation from a commercial shipbuilder into a potential supplier for the U.S. defense industrial base. Ras Tanura, which has a capacity of 550,000 barrels per day, was shut for a period in the early months of the Iran war as a precautionary measure. articles.title: Fugro wins UXO survey contract for German offshore grid connections
articles.summary: Fugro has been awarded a contract by 50Hertz to deliver unexploded ordnance (UXO) survey, identification and clearance services for the LanWin3...
articles.body: Cabling October 27, 2026 · 4 hours ago Fugro wins UXO survey contract for German offshore grid connections 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Fugro Fugro has been awarded a contract by 50Hertz to deliver unexploded ordnance (UXO) survey, identification and clearance services for the LanWin3 and LanWin6 offshore grid connection projects in the German sector of the North Sea. By identifying and addressing potential hazards, the work will help 50Hertz prepare the routes for the safe installation of high-voltage direct current (HVDC) cables connecting offshore wind farms to Germany’s electricity network. LanWin3 and LanWin6 form part of Germany’s ongoing expansion of its offshore wind energy infrastructure. Once completed, each grid connection is designed to transmit up to 2 GW of offshore wind power, providing a combined transmission capacity of 4 GW and helping bring more renewable electricity from the North Sea into the national grid to build energy security and meet climate targets. Starting in the second quarter of 2027, the UXO survey will cover 200-meter-wide corridors along the LanWin3 and LanWin6 routes. The work will be carried out using two Geowing systems, Fugro's fixed magnetic gradiometer arrays, each fitted with ten magnetic sensors to detect potential UXO and other objects on or beneath the seabed. The survey will provide the geo-data needed to map potential targets and create a master target list for further investigation. Follow-on inspection and identification activities will take place in 2028, using remotely operated vehicle (ROV) technology and specialist detection systems to investigate selected targets and remove debris where required. Fugro will also support the safe removal and disposal of any confirmed UXO in accordance with regulatory requirements, helping prepare the cable corridors for installation. "On a project of this scale, the challenge is that the number and nature of potential UXO can only be known once the survey is complete. Building a reliable picture of the seabed at an early stage will allow 50Hertz to plan the next steps with greater certainty and manage safety throughout the cable installation programme," said Ronny Bøhn, Fugro’s Director of Marine Geophysics for Europe and Africa. articles.body: Seatrium, Karpowership Link Up on Floating Power and Digital Infrastructure Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 27, 2026 © Seatrium Seatrium announced that it has entered into a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with global floating power solutions specialist Karpowership to pursue a joint venture to develop floating power and infrastructure solutions in Singapore, with the potential to extend cooperation to the wider Southeast Asia market. The two companies will create an integrated platform combining infrastructure development, financing, engineering, construction and operations. The collaboration brings together Seatrium’s global offshore engineering, procurement and construction and systems integration capabilities with Karpowership’s expertise in developing, financing, owning and operating floating power and digital infrastructure, alongside its experience in delivering behind-the-meter power solutions for super intelligence. Announced at Singapore International Energy Week (SIEW) 2026 and witnessed by Dr. Tan See Leng, Singapore’s Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry), the MoU establishes a framework to jointly develop rapidly deployable power and infrastructure solutions in Singapore, which may include Powerships, floating data centers, turbine-based or hybrid vessels and floating nuclear solutions. The partners share a longer-term ambition to bolster Singapore’s position to serve as a resilient regional hub for rapidly deployable energy and digital infrastructure solutions. Today, Singapore remains heavily reliant on imported natural gas, which accounts for approximately 95% of its electricity generation, according to the Energy Market Authority. Continued disruptions to global fuel supplies have reinforced the need for diversifying energy sources and strengthening the resilience of Singapore's electricity system. At the same time, EMA estimates that Singapore's peak electricity demand is projected to grow between 2.4% and 4.8% annually to reach up to 11.4 gigawatts by 2031, driven in part by transport electrification and the expansion of energy-intensive industries on the island, including semiconductor manufacturing and data centres. Across Southeast Asia, the similar growth of digital industries has also led to increased infrastructure requirements. According to the 9 th ASEAN Energy Outlook, 20% of ASEAN's projected electricity demand growth in the next five years will be attributable to data centres. This, compounded with structural drivers of industrialisation and urbanisation, emphasise the need for reliable power to support industrial activity and other energy-intensive facilities. Against this backdrop, floating power infrastructure could provide additional options to enhance supply security, including through the rapid deployment of generation capacity, contingency power provision and support for critical infrastructure, including data centers. Such solutions, including the potential use of emerging energies such as hydrogen, could also offer flexibility in deployment locations, enable power generation assets to be adapted or redeployed, and chart a longer-term transition pathway as energy requirements continue to evolve. This MoU represents a new phase in the companies’ relationship. Since 2018, Seatrium has delivered seven FSRU conversions to Karpowership, with the 8 th and 9 th unit awarded this year, supporting the deployment of Karpowership’s LNG-to-power solutions across international markets. Seatrium has most recently secured a contract in October for the development and integration of Karpowership’s hydrogen-ready third-generation Whale Class Powerships to be deployed in countries requiring reliable energy supply.

articles.title: ANYbotics Delivers Explosion-Protected Inspection Robots for Offshore Energy
articles.summary: Swiss robotics company ANYbotics has begun customer deliveries of ANYmal X, a four-legged autonomous inspection robot designed to operate in potentially explosive environments, opening new opportunities for robotic inspection across offshore…
articles.body: ANYbotics Delivers Explosion-Protected Inspection Robots for Offshore Energy Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 27, 2026 Image courtesy ANYbotics Image courtesy ANYbotics Swiss robotics company ANYbotics has begun customer deliveries of ANYmal X, a four-legged autonomous inspection robot designed to operate in potentially explosive environments, opening new opportunities for robotic inspection across offshore oil and gas installations and industrial processing facilities. Initial customers include Equinor and DSM-Firmenich , following an extensive testing program involving BP, Shell, PETRONAS, Petrobras, BASF and SLB . Since 2023, participating companies have evaluated the technology across hundreds of onshore and offshore inspection missions. ANYmal X is engineered to meet ATEX and IECEx explosion-protection standards, addressing a major obstacle to deploying autonomous mobile robots in hazardous areas containing flammable gases or vapors. The robot navigates stairs, narrow walkways and complex industrial infrastructure without requiring facility modifications. Integrated thermal, visual, acoustic and gas sensors monitor pumps, compressors, valves and piping for overheating, leaks, abnormal noise and equipment deterioration. "Many experts thought a legged robot could never be made safe for explosive atmospheres," said Péter Fankhauser, Co-Founder and CEO of ANYbotics . "That changes today." Developing the system required four years of engineering and resulted in more than 10 patents, according to the company. Explosion-protection measures include nitrogen-filled sealed chambers housing electronics and inspection equipment, flameproof enclosures protecting the battery and 12 leg actuators, conductive feet for grounding and automatic temperature monitoring. ANYmal X operates through ANYbotics' Shift platform, which schedules autonomous inspection rounds, associates collected measurements with individual assets and integrates findings into existing maintenance management systems, including SAP, Yokogawa and SLB platforms. The technology is intended to reduce personnel exposure to hazardous operating environments while providing repeatable equipment condition data for predictive maintenance and digital twin applications. ANYbotics reports that its existing industrial inspection systems conduct more than 120,000 autonomous inspections monthly across over 50 customers in power, metals and materials industries. The company will publicly demonstrate ANYmal X and its industrial AI platform alongside SLB and Kuwait Oil Company at ADIPEC 2026, November 2–5, in Abu Dhabi. Image courtesy ANYbotics

articles.title: Norway Grants Funding to Advance Nuclear Propulsion for Ships
articles.summary: The Research Council of Norway has awarded $2 million (NOK 20 million) in initial funding to the Emerald Nuclear Norway-led Marine Nuclear Propulsion System (MarNuPS) project, which aims to develop and test an integrated nuclear propulsion system for offshore vessels…
articles.body: Norway Grants Funding to Advance Nuclear Propulsion for Ships Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 27, 2026 (Credit: Emerald Nuclear Norway) The Research Council of Norway has awarded $2 million (NOK 20 million) in initial funding to the Emerald Nuclear Norway-led Marine Nuclear Propulsion System (MarNuPS) project, which aims to develop and test an integrated nuclear propulsion system for offshore vessels, with first deployment targeted for 2031-32. The project brings together Emerald Nuclear Norway, VARD Group, Vard Electro, Island Offshore, NTNU, Imperial College London and Maskindynamikk to advance maritime nuclear propulsion from system development towards physical integration and testing. The funding comes alongside substantial investment from the project partners, with the first stage of the program estimated to cost around $15. 6 million (NOK 150 million). MarNuPS will integrate Emerald Nuclear's 5 MWe Gem Microreactor technology with energy storage, power conversion, vessel power management, automation and bridge control systems. The first stage, planned for 2027, will involve establishing an integrated test facility at Stette, outside Ålesund, where a full-scale representation of the shipboard propulsion system will be assembled and tested. The facility will use electric heating instead of nuclear fuel, allowing the project partners to evaluate how the different systems operate together under conditions representative of vessel operations. Testing will cover normal operations, rapid changes in power demand, transient and stress conditions, system performance and crew interaction. “The partners are already making a substantial commitment to MarNuPS, and this support gives the programme additional backing as we move from design and analysis towards building and testing a complete integrated system. It's only the beginning of a longer development and qualification process, but it demonstrates that maritime nuclear propulsion is now being pursued as a serious industrial project,” said Hallgeir Juliebø, Co-Founder and Chief Commercial Officer of Emerald Nuclear and Chairman of Emerald Nuclear Norway. Emerald Nuclear's Gem Microreactor is designed for ships and floating remote-power applications. Under the company's proposed leasing model, Emerald Nuclear would retain ownership and operation of the reactor and responsibility for the fuel cycle, while shipowners would purchase the power. Island Offshore plans to become the first shipowner to install the reactor and energy system, with deployment targeted for 2031-32. “Nuclear energy has the potential to provide a new route to decarbonizing offshore vessels without compromising the power, endurance and operational flexibility these ships require,” added Tommy Walaunet, CEO of Island Offshore. The project partners will contribute expertise across reactor technology, ship design, power management, vessel operations, nuclear modelling, structural integrity and condition monitoring. MarNuPS builds on earlier Norwegian research into maritime nuclear propulsion, including the NTNU-led NuProShip program, and forms part of the demonstration work linked to SFI SAINT national research center.

articles.body: ABS Verifies HD KSOE, HHI Breakerless Marine Power System Concept Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 27, 2026 (Credit: ABS) HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering (HD KSOE) and HD Hyundai Heavy Industries (HHI) have secured concept verification from the American Bureau of Shipping (ABS) for a breakerless medium-voltage direct current (MVDC) power system designed to improve energy efficiency and support electrification of large commercial vessels. The system, designed for vessels requiring around 30 MW of power, aims to improve energy efficiency and support high-capacity electrification as ships grow larger and require more powerful electrical distribution systems. The breakerless MVDC architecture integrates advanced control and fault-management capabilities to support safe and resilient power distribution. The milestone follows the completion of the technology's Feasibility Stage in 2025, as part of a joint development project launched in 2024 to explore the application of MVDC power systems onboard ships. “Large vessels are asking more of their power systems, and MVDC offers a promising route to higher efficiency and greater capacity. This work with HD KSOE and HHI gives owners and yards a clearer view of the technology’s potential and supports the development of ABS guidance for MVDC,” said Patrick Ryan, ABS Senior Vice President and Chief Technology Officer. Following the latest verification milestone, the development will move towards Prototype Validation, the next stage in advancing the technology for maritime applications. “With the Feasibility Stage completed in 2025 and Concept Verification now secured, our timeline for delivering advanced marine MVDC systems is rapidly accelerating. As we move toward Prototype Validation, we are committed to perfecting this breakerless technology and setting a new standard for safe, high-power electrification in the maritime industry,” added Sang-Hyun Kim, Senior Vice President of the Electrification Center at HD KSOE. ABS is also working with technology developers and shipbuilders to establish technical guidance supporting the wider adoption of high-capacity electrification in the maritime industry.

articles.summary: By- Nisha Lathif, General Manager, Oil and Gas,Honeywell Technologies With decades of expertise in addressing the complex needs of the energy...
articles.body: Branded Content October 27, 2026 · 5 hours ago Accelerating operational excellence in offshore energy Written in partnership with Honeywell Technologies 6 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Integrated offshore solutions by Honeywell Technologies @Honeywell Technologies By- Nisha Lathif, General Manager, Oil and Gas,Honeywell Technologies With decades of expertise in addressing the complex needs of the energy sector in challenging marine environments, Honeywell Technologies is at the heart of shaping the future of offshore energy operations. Our advances are supporting a fundamental shift in the industry, helping transform traditional offshore operations into becoming more connected, intelligent and data driven. As digital technologies continue to evolve, we see that operators can leverage real-time data, advanced analytics and integrated operational platforms to gain deeper insights into asset performance and operational efficiency. This shift is enabling organizations to make more informed decisions, optimize maintenance and production strategies and create more agile, resilient offshore operations. Offshore operations are entering a new era Offshore energy operators are confronting a convergence of pressures that traditional ways of working were never designed to handle. Aging infrastructure is becoming a primary constraint today. While equipment ages, operational complexity continues to increase, experienced offshore professionals are becoming harder to replace and the pressure to improve reliability and safety while managing costs remains high. 4,5 The key to solving many of these challenges can be found in data. Modern offshore facilities generate massive volumes of operational data. Historically, much of this information was underutilized, trapped in individual systems or available only after issues had already occurred. Some operators are now moving beyond traditional maintenance strategies to embrace digital technologies that enable smarter, faster operational decision-making. The organizations making the greatest progress are those that convert operational data into actionable intelligence. Rather than simply collecting information, they are using analytics and connected systems to identify risks earlier, optimize maintenance activities and improve operational performance before failures impact production. Why predictive operations matter Reactive and time-based maintenance have clear limitations. Waiting for equipment to fail means unplanned downtime, lost production and elevated safety risk. Servicing equipment on a fixed calendar schedule, regardless of actual condition, wastes resources and can compromise assets through unnecessary intervention. Condition-based maintenance (CBM) offers a proactive alternative, focusing on real-time monitoring rather than adherence to fixed schedules. Operational and equipment data are continuously monitored to assess actual asset health. By combining real-time monitoring with advanced analytics, operators can identify emerging issues before they develop into significant failures. The benefits of this approach are substantial: · Reduced unplanned downtime · Better maintenance prioritization · Improved equipment availability · Reduced operational risk · Enhanced workforce productivity By assessing the actual state of equipment, operators can conduct maintenance only when conditions warrant it, effectively reducing unnecessary downtime and optimizing resource allocation. CBM moves beyond simple data collection. When data, analytics and human expertise are connected, operators gain the ability to move from reacting to problems toward anticipating and preventing them. That helps people make faster, better decisions. Aker BP: A case study of CBM in offshore operations 2, 3 Aker BP, a leading energy exploration and production company operating on the Norwegian Continental Shelf, offers a practical illustration of CBM in action. Like many offshore producers, their challenges included managing equipment reliability and conducting maintenance across multiple offshore assets while maintaining high safety standards and operational efficiency. To overcome these challenges Aker BP adopted condition-based maintenance using Honeywell Technologies Forge Asset Performance Management (APM), a connected platform that integrates real-time data from multiple equipment types and original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) into a single dashboard, creating a unified, OEM-agnostic approach to asset health monitoring that facilitates proactive decision-making. With Honeywell Technologies Forge APM now providing enterprise-wide control, Aker BP can continuously monitor equipment conditions on six of its assets in the North Sea, ensuring that maintenance is carried out only when necessary. Aker BP reports that the real benefits of using CBM strategies have been meaningful: · Earlier identification of equipment issues · Reduced dependence on manual inspections · Better prioritization of maintenance activities · Improved situational awareness In addition, equipment essential for safety—such as safety valves, pressure sensors and critical control systems — receives focused attention based on its operational status. The new approach also carries clear safety benefits for Aker BP. By reducing the frequency of scheduled maintenance (some of it unnecessary), CBM minimizes disruptions to their ongoing operations, thereby decreasing the chances of accidents during maintenance activities. The advantages gained were not simply from software deployment. Dedicated ownership and continuous refinement were also essential. Experienced technicians at Aker BP set up their own models in the system specifically for their required calculations. They engaged ongoing improvement and adaptation to the monitoring process that allowed engineers to tune the system more effectively, minimize false alerts and concentrate on critical issues. This is a reminder that predictive maintenance is fundamentally a new operating model. Success requires connected data, advanced analytics and experienced personnel working together to make better decisions. Technology provides visibility and insight, but operational excellence still depends on informed human judgment. Lessons for the offshore industry The Aker BP experience points to several broader ideals for the offshore industry: · Connect data across systems. Operators need a unified view instead of isolated monitoring tools. Integrating data from multiple equipment types and OEMs into a single dashboard enables proactive decision-making. · Focus on actionable insights. The goal is not more alerts—the goal is better decisions. Minimizing false alerts keeps attention on critical issues. · Combine technology and expertise . Analytics support engineers, but people remain central to decision-making. · Create a culture of continuous improvement. Condition-monitoring systems become more valuable as teams refine models and operating practices over time. Building the offshore operation of the future Putting these ideals into practice to create future-ready offshore operations requires an integrated operating environment that connects production systems, assets, people, safety functions and sustainability objectives. Honeywell Technologies engages in all aspects of transforming offshore operations through six connected domains that collectively support safer, more efficient and more resilient offshore production. For the operational foundation we bring operations and control capabilities, including SCADA, process control, telemetry and connectivity that provide visibility across offshore assets. We enable digital transformation technologies such as Industrial IoT, predictive analytics, AI-enabled operations and digital twins to help organizations transform data into operational intelligence. Honeywell Technologies asset performance solutions support reliability and optimization through asset performance management platforms, turbomachinery optimization, measurement technologies and energy management capabilities. Our people and collaboration technologies enable remote operations, expert collaboration, knowledge management and workforce training, addressing the growing workforce challenges across offshore operations. Our safety and security systems integrate process safety, cybersecurity, and fire and gas systems into a unified operational environment. We compliment these with sustainability solutions that incorporate emissions monitoring, energy optimization and carbon management capabilities. The entire portfolio of Honeywell Technologies’ offshore production capabilities creates a connected operational ecosystem where data flows across functions, enabling faster decisions, improved efficiency and greater resilience. The next frontier of operational excellence As the Aker BP example demonstrates, the real value of offshore operational excellence lies not in technology alone, but in transforming operational data into actionable insights. By connecting assets, people and processes within a unified operational environment, operators can improve reliability, enhance efficiency and support safer operations. As the industry evolves, condition-based maintenance and predictive analytics will continue to play a key role in building more resilient and high-performing offshore operations. articles.body: Saudi Arabia, Greece call for safe shipping routes, closer energy ties in Hellenic Shipping News 27/10/2026 Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis held talks in Riyadh, pledging to deepen cooperation on energy, investment and digital connectivity as the countries marked 100 years of diplomatic relations. The crown prince received Mitsotakis at Al-Yamamah Palace, where an official reception ceremony preceded the talks, the Saudi Press Agency reported. In a joint statement issued at the end of the visit, both sides stressed the need to protect international shipping routes and keep energy supplies flowing without interruption. They expressed concern about attacks on energy infrastructure and their effects on supplies and market stability. Greece praised Saudi efforts to stabilize global oil markets and maintain supplies through alternative export routes, including the East-West Pipeline. The discussions also focused on expanding economic ties. The countries said bilateral trade reached about $1.7 billion in 2025, up from 2021, and called for stronger investment ties in infrastructure, construction, energy, logistics and technology. The talks built on a strategic partnership council announced during the crown prince’s visit to Greece in July 2022. The council held its first meeting during Mitsotakis’ visit to Saudi Arabia in January 2025. Among their energy priorities, the two countries pledged to accelerate work on the planned Saudi-Greek electricity interconnection. The project aims to enable electricity exchanges, improve grid reliability and strengthen power links between Saudi Arabia and Europe through Greece. They also agreed to explore opportunities to export clean hydrogen from Saudi Arabia to Greece and other European Union markets, while expanding investment in conventional and renewable energy and petrochemicals. Beyond energy, the two sides welcomed progress on the EMC submarine cable project, designed to strengthen digital connectivity between East and West, and pledged to coordinate its completion according to the agreed timetable. Saudi Arabia encouraged Greek companies to establish regional headquarters in the Kingdom and pursue opportunities linked to major projects, including Riyadh Expo 2030 and the 2034 FIFA World Cup. Greece, in turn, invited Saudi investment in energy, transport, logistics, digital infrastructure and advanced technologies, highlighting its position as a gateway to European markets. The two countries also pledged closer defense and security cooperation, including efforts to combat crime, terrorism and terrorist financing. They called for greater exchanges of expertise and training, along with cybersecurity cooperation and information sharing. On climate policy, both sides reaffirmed their commitment to the principles of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Paris Agreement. They also supported cooperation on the circular carbon economy, an approach to managing carbon emissions. The statement outlined further areas for cooperation, including artificial intelligence, space technology, health, education, culture, tourism and sports. Earlier on Sunday, Mitsotakis was received by the deputy governor of the Riyadh region, Prince Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Abdulaziz. Source: Arab News 2026-10-27 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Nuclear ships only pay off under the IMO’s net-zero rules, UCL study finds
articles.summary: Nuclear propulsion can compete in container shipping only if an effective global emissions policy is in place and reactor costs fall sharply, according to new research from the UCL Energy Institute’s Shipping and Oceans Research Group. It is one of the most detailed total cost-of-ownership assessments of nuclear...
articles.body: Nuclear ships only pay off under the IMO’s net-zero rules, UCL study finds in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 27/10/2026 Nuclear propulsion can compete in container shipping only if an effective global emissions policy is in place and reactor costs fall sharply, according to new research from the UCL Energy Institute’s Shipping and Oceans Research Group. It is one of the most detailed total cost-of-ownership assessments of nuclear merchant shipping to date. The report, Nuclear Reactors for Merchant Shipping: A Total Cost of Ownership Assessment of a Low-Carbon Pathway, compares a large container ship (14,500 to 19,999 TEU) with nuclear propulsion against conventional fuel oil and dual-fuel ammonia vessels. It uses a literature review, interviews with five UK-based experts in law, insurance, classification, technology development and industry representation, and a cost model run with and without the IMO Net-Zero Framework (NZF). Key findings ● Policy sets the business case. Without the NZF, no nuclear vessel is cheaper than a conventional ship, even at the lowest assumed reactor cost. Under the NZF, nuclear vessels earn income by selling surplus units to other ships, which closes the gap. ● Reactor cost decides the outcome. Published estimates range from about 2,600 to 12,400 USD per kWe, a spread of nearly five times. At the low end, which assumes series production and deep cost reductions, nuclear is the cheapest option from 2040. At the high end, which reflects first-of-a-kind reactors, it is not cheapest in any scenario. ● The window is narrow. Surplus unit income is largest when a vessel enters service and shrinks as the NZF’s fuel targets tighten. Nuclear’s best chance to break into the market is early, not late. ● Faster is not cheaper. At 25 knots, the vessel sails 32% more distance a year but needs more than three times the installed power, and costs rise. ● Non-technical barriers are as large as the technical ones. Existing nuclear liability conventions were designed for fixed, land-based reactors. Interviewees expect no global framework for the first vessels, and a mature insurance regime could take 15 to 20 years. “Nuclear can compete, but only with much cheaper reactors and a global emissions policy, and neither exists yet. How both develop over the coming years will decide whether nuclear has a place in shipping.” said Farah Bziker, Researcher, UCL Shipping and Oceans Research Group. Three features of the NZF support nuclear as a maritime energy source: a stringent fuel-intensity limit or steep reduction rate to ensure long-term demand; a stable, high-integrity surplus-unit market with a firm price; and a strong, sustained reward for zero- and near-zero-emission technologies. Policy that is less ambitious or less supportive of these technologies than the NZF will reduce nuclear’s potential. “Nuclear is not a reason to weaken maritime climate policy. It is one of the technologies that depends on it. Anyone backing reactor programmes should want a stringent international GHG policy and credible global framework,” said Dr Tristan Smith, Professor of Energy and Transport, UCL Shipping and Oceans Research Group. The authors caution that the results may understate the true cost of nuclear shipping. The model excludes nuclear-specific insurance, reactor maintenance and hull integration, and treats decommissioning as a rough estimate. Vessels with first-of-a-kind reactors are not competitive, and it remains open who would bear their cost. A favourable cost comparison is also not enough: the first vessels will need agreements between states on liability, insurance and regulation. Key findings ● Policy sets the business case.
Without the NZF, no nuclear vessel is cheaper than a conventional ship, even at the lowest assumed reactor cost.

articles.body: Industry Leaders Launch World’s First Maritime-Specific Cyber Vulnerabilities Database in International Shipping News 27/10/2026 Cydome, ClassNK, Bureau Veritas, MTS-ISAC and Rakuten Maritime announced today a collaboration called the Blue Initiative to provide the first public database of cyber vulnerabilities focused only on IT and OT devices that are relevant to the maritime industry, available for free at blue-initiative.org. With the rising number of vulnerabilities discoveries (more than 350,000 published CVEs and 200 entries added each day), identifying and prioritizing which system patches and cyber risks are relevant to each organization has become an extremely complex endeavor. This new initiative is designed to help shipping companies more effectively address the cyber vulnerabilities affecting the specific systems and equipment they operate by highlighting maritime-related equipment, ability to focus on specific vendors, and proactively alerting users when relevant new vulnerabilities are announced. “Identifying which vulnerabilities actually matter to the systems maritime companies operate is a major challenge”, said Cydome CEO Nir Ayalon, “and our vision with the Blue Initiative is to have a public and open single source of truth for maritime-related vulnerabilities. This will provide IT and cyber teams, vendors and research facilities a much more focused view of risks relevant to their specific vessels, making vulnerabilities and risk management much more effective and faster than before. “ The Blue Initiative is an open industry collaboration, freely accessible at blue-initiative.org. Relevant organizations in the maritime community are encouraged to join and help expand the database. Effective vulnerability management starts with knowing which issues matter to the systems you operate. By focusing on maritime IT and OT equipment and bringing the community together to validate the data, the Blue Initiative gives shipping companies a practical, trusted resource. ClassNK is proud to be a contributing partner,” said Naoki Saito, General Manager, Ship Management Systems Department at ClassNK Cyber resilience requirements for ships are not simply a checklist for audits, but a continuous process throughout a vessel’s operational life. Owners are expected to maintain the security of onboard systems as new vulnerabilities emerge, making effective vulnerability management a critical element of maritime cyber resilience. In practice, this can be challenging, as relevant information is often scattered across general-purpose databases and vendor advisories. Bureau Veritas sees real value in a shared, maritime-specific reference that owners, equipment manufacturers and class societies can all rely on. We are pleased to join the Blue Initiative as a contributing partner,” said Panagiotis Anastasiou , Cyber Technical & Market Leader, Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore. Amid a shifting threat landscape where technological advancement increasingly empowers threat actors targeting maritime critical infrastructure, The Blue Initiative delivers essential vulnerability intelligence that addresses a critical vulnerability gap. Recognizing the value of this community-driven approach to maritime situational awareness, the MTS-ISAC strongly endorses this collaborative model and has integrated its operational workflows to both contribute to and leverage this vital initiative,” said Christy Coffey, VP Operations at MTS-ISAC. Cybersecurity must be managed across a vessel’s entire operational lifecycle, from design through operation. As a provider of maritime cybersecurity, compliance, and digital solutions, Rakuten Maritime knows that tracking equipment vulnerabilities is critical to keeping connected fleets secure. By turning complex threat intelligence into actionable protection, the Blue Initiative gives operators the trusted reference they need, and we are proud to be a contributing partner,” said Ryan Son, Managing Director of Rakuten Symphony Singapore & Korea and Head of Rakuten Maritime. Entries in the new Maritime Vulnerabilities Repository (MVR) are reviewed by cyber researchers from Cydome and the contributing partners, who validate and refine them before going live. Select entries also receive more elaborate analyst notes, and users will be able to: Browse vulnerabilities and their details Filter vulnerability searches to the equipment or vendors relevant to them. Access expert insights on vulnerabilities and their impact (select vulnerabilities, with more insights constantly added every day). Subscribe for updates and alerts on new vulnerabilities. “In most cases, vulnerabilities are only published once a patch is available, in line with standard responsible disclosure processes,” said Ayalon. “But the Blue Initiative links this intelligence to the specific vendors and systems that maritime users operate, allowing them to move quickly to patch and mitigate.
