articles.body: LNG shipping stocks: Qatar goes shopping in International Shipping News 27/10/2026 The UP World LNG Shipping Index fell 3.43 points (1.53%) to close at 221.48, a more moderate retreat than the prior week, while the S&P 500 lost 0.47%. Unlike recent weeks, the internals were soft too: the median fell 1.79% and the weighted index (wUPI) dropped 3.27%, with breadth of 8:13. The dominant story was news flow rather than price: QatarEnergy signed major long-term US supply deals — up to 4 mtpa from Cheniere through 2054, plus advanced talks with Woodside (up to 3 mtpa) and Venture Global — to cover its war-induced liquefaction outages, and the first Qatari cargo since April headed via the Red Sea to Poland’s Świnoujście terminal. ALNG led the gainers (+12%), with Tsakos +4.5% and the oil & gas majors (Chevron +3.65%, BP +2.2%, Shell +1.43%) all at fresh yearly highs. The fallers were led by New Fortress Energy (−16%, new lows), COSCO (−8.37%) and Pan Ocean (−8%), with ADNOC −7.25% and Korea Line −6.8%. In the background, gas prices rose in both basins on colder weather and strong Chinese spot buying — Asian LNG to $30.50/MMBtu, Europe just over $29 — while spot tanker rates firmed on Pacific routes to $30,750 (Atlantic $21,750). UPI & SPX The UP World LNG Shipping Index, which tracks 21 listed LNG shipping companies, lost 3.43 points (1.53%) to close at 221.48 points, while the S&P 500 index lost 0.47%. The chart below illustrates the performance of both indices with weekly data. Week 43-2026: Chart of the UP World LNG Shipping Index with S&P 500 (Source: UP-Indices) Broader View The UPI continues to fall at a more moderate pace. The median fall was 1.79 per cent, whilst the weighted index (wUPI) fell by 3.27 per cent. The ratio of rising to falling companies was 8:13. The UPI is being weighed down by uncertainty in the stock market and growing signs of a resumption of US strikes against Iran, while positive factors include the weather, rising demand for gas and, in the longer term, new Qatari contracts for US gas. Some interesting news emerged at the end of the week. The biggest surprise came in the form of a statement by the former CEO of Polar LNG to the Financial Times, revealing that Russia’s Novatek is behind the Alaskan project. The second piece of news concerned new LNG supply contracts signed by QatarEnergy with US and Australian companies. QatarEnergy is thus addressing the war-induced outages in its liquefaction capacity. QatarEnergy has signed two long-term deals to buy up to 4 mtpa of LNG from Cheniere Energy under agreements extending into the second half of the century, according to TradeWinds. Bloomberg first reported the news. Reuters reported on the second contract with the Australian company Woodside. A long-term deal could cover up to 3 million metric tonnes a year for 15 to 20 years, according to one source. Woodside’s Louisiana LNG plant, currently under construction, has an export capacity of 16.5 mtpa. QatarEnergy also holds a 70 per cent stake in the Golden Pass LNG facility being developed in Louisiana, which, when complete, will have the capacity to export up to 18 mtpa of LNG. Louisiana LNG is said to be asking for a premium on liquefaction fees exceeding $2.50 per mmBtu and above average US market prices due to contractual flexibility, offering potential buyers shorter contracts in return for higher prices, two people told Reuters. Reuters also reported on Thursday that QatarEnergy is in advanced talks with Venture Global (VG.N), opens new tab, regarding a long-term supply deal to purchase at least 3 million metric tonnes of LNG per year. Thirdly, Energy Intelligence reported on Qatari gas heading via the Red Sea to Poland. This is the first shipment since April. It is a Qatar-Max-sized tanker. It is worth recalling a piece of information a Czech expert shared with me. Originally, the Nord Stream pipeline was to be constructed in such a way as to prevent these ships from reaching Poland. However, the Poles realised this in time, and the Russians had to make adjustments. Energy decisions have long-term implications. The vessel’s latest Automatic Identification System (AIS) signal listed Poland’s Świnoujście import terminal as its destination, with an estimated arrival date of 14 November. This suggests the cargo is being delivered to the Polish firm Orlen under its long-term contract with QatarEnergy. However, the apparent delivery raises further questions, given that Orlen’s two separate long-term contracts with QatarEnergy are understood to remain under force majeure. The Qatari state exporter declared force majeure following the outbreak of the Gulf War and subsequent drone attacks against its Ras Laffan industrial complex in March. LNG imports from Qatar accounted for less than 10 per cent of the demand generated by Orlen and its gas customers in 2025, the company told Energy Intelligence earlier this year. A weekly Reuters round-up reported on rising gas prices in both Asia and Europe, driven by cooler weather as well as higher consumption and demand: Asian LNG prices rose to $30.50 per MMBtu, whilst European prices climbed to just over $29 per MMBtu. “Colder weather forecast across Europe in early November could accelerate storage withdrawals. Northeast Asia also faces colder-than-normal forecasts, although ample inventories should limit near-term LNG competition, with risks shifting towards later months as stocks decline,” said Kesher Sumeet, senior analyst at Energy Aspects. Asian demand has risen more sharply than European demand this week, intensifying competition between basins, said Martin Senior, head of LNG pricing at Argus. Chinese spot demand has been strong over the past week, with the state-owned CNOOC purchasing at least 11 cargoes and negotiating for further volumes in November and December to meet storage targets, whilst South Korea’s Kogas was also seeking volumes, he added. China has already experienced a sharp drop in temperatures in its northern and north-eastern regions, with temperatures forecast to fall across its central and eastern areas, whilst South Korea is also seeing colder air moving in, said Rystad Energy analyst Mathieu Utting in a note. “If this cooling proves sustained, spot LNG buying from China and South Korea will accelerate, and European buyers will need to raise their bids to secure the Atlantic cargoes they are counting on for the winter,” he said. European LNG markets rose over the week amid geopolitical developments in the Middle East, Norwegian pipeline outages and demand from Egypt, which is seeking five LNG cargoes for delivery in November, said Aly Blakeway, head of Atlantic LNG at S&P Global Energy. Spot rates rose mainly for Pacific routes, reaching $30,750 per day. Atlantic rates stood at $21,750, according to Spark Commodities. According to our UPI TCE, the average UPI contracts are now around $70,000 per day. Constituents The only double-digit gain last week was posted by ALNG (OSE: ALNG), which rose by 12 per cent. This represented a move from the lower end of the trading range to the upper end, accompanied by above-average trading volume. It must be acknowledged, however, that the average trading volume is quite low. The second-highest gain was just 4.5 per cent, posted by Tsakos Energy Navigation (NYSE: TEN). This move also took the price to the upper edge of the range and above the resistance level of the closing prices, although it ended at a key resistance level. Compared with the negative candlestick of the week before last, this is a positive candlestick (with a shadow). However, volume was only average. The trio of oil and gas companies, which also operate in the complementary LNG maritime transport sector, took the next three places in the growth rankings. Compared with the week before last, the gains were smaller. Chevron (NYSE: CVX) gained 3.65 per cent, BP (NYSE: BP) rose by 2.2 per cent and Shell (NYSE: SHEL) by 1.43 per cent. Nevertheless, all three have reached new highs for the year, well above their spring prices. Trading volumes were average to slightly below average. FLEX LNG (NYSE: FLNG) posted the only gain of more than one per cent. Although small in percentage terms, this rise is significant as it occurred at a support level following a break below the $30 mark. During the week, FLNG corrected further, down to $27, but ultimately returned above $28.50. This is a level identified and confirmed in February, July and now. Golar LNG (NASDAQ: GLNG) showed the latest positive movement. The 0.77 per cent rise followed a similar pattern to FLNG, though the support level is not as clearly visible. The price entered the range of summer 2025 prices but remained at its upper limits, perhaps even just above them. This level has therefore been rejected for now; we will see whether it rises to the $50 mark. Paradoxically, Dynagas LNG Partners (NYSE: DLNG) confirmed its previous 3.3 per cent decline with a 0.6 per cent rise. New Fortress Energy (NASDAQ: NFE) once again leads the fallers, having lost 16 per cent and hit new lows. There were two shares down by 8 per cent: COSCO Shipping Energy Transportation (SS: 600026; -8.37 per cent) and Pan Ocean (KRX: 028670; -8 per cent). Whilst Pan Ocean corrected its previous break above resistance by returning to its upper boundary, COSCO is correcting its previous rise for the second week running. The question is whether the rise itself was a correction and the trend is now continuing downwards, as there are several possible interpretations. On the one hand, the price has fallen out of the sideways range seen in the spring (negative view); on the other hand, this may be a continuation of the downtrend from the spring (a lower high has formed, negative view), or it may be a correction within an uptrend, after which the price will return to those spring levels (positive view). We do not know and will leave further developments to the market. ADNOC Logistics & Services (ADX: ADNOCLS) fell 7.25 per cent, ending its clearly positive run with a pullback to a lower level. Even so, the overall trend remains positive, and the decline may not continue. Korea Line Corporation (KRX: 005880) broke out of its sideways range by breaching support. It fell by 6.8 per cent. MISC (KLSE: 3816; -5.3 per cent) saw a correction following the previous week’s gains. The decline was somewhat mitigated, but the share price remained, albeit just barely, within the summer’s sideways trend. Nakilat (QSE: QGTS; -3.71 per cent) and Exmar (EBR: EXM; -3 per cent) both fell by three per cent. We have covered the development of Qatari exports in sufficient detail in the previous section. Nakilat fell but staged a positive recovery, so the decline was not as severe as during the week. Nevertheless, it remains within the price range seen in 2023. Exmar continues its sideways trend slightly below its highest prices. Excelerate Energy (NYSE: EE) once again found support at $32.4. The decline was 2.4 per cent. The Japanese trio continues to perform similarly, with losses of around 1.85 per cent. NYK Line (TSE: 9101), Mitsui O.S.K. Lines (TSE: 9104) and “K” Line (TSE: 9107) continue to move sideways near their highs for the year. Capital Clean Energy Carriers (NASDAQ: CCEC) is also trading near support within a sideways range. The share price fell by 0.7 per cent. Crystal Ball Qatar remains sidelined among the conflict’s losers — but the key constraint is export, not production. The damage to Ras Laffan removed around 17% of capacity (two of 14 trains), which QatarEnergy expects to take three to five years to repair. The remaining ~80% of capacity is intact and could, in principle, return to market — but the Strait of Hormuz is Qatar’s sole export route, and executives (including Shell’s) caution that even a reopening would not restore pre-war flows overnight, as high war-risk insurance continues to deter tanker returns to the Gulf. For now, this keeps a large share of Qatari volume bottled up, and US LNG exporters emerge as the clear winners. European importers were shielded from spot price increases largely because of long-term US contracts; however, these are not enough to replenish winter inventories, and European companies must return to the market despite Qatar’s continuing export restrictions. We expect most of the rising US gas production to flow toward Europe. New global LNG producers should also benefit, as energy source diversification becomes more important than ever — provided importing economies remain healthy enough to absorb higher energy costs. The outlook remains volatile, but positive in the long term. The gradual phasing out of steam vessels and the addition of new liquefaction capacity will continue to drive the sector forward. articles.title: EU marine protected areas: the challenge of turning the tide from paper to the sea
articles.summary: The EU’s marine protected areas often fail to receive effective protection, and the EU is unlikely to meet its 2030 marine conservation targets, according to a new report by the European Court of Auditors (ECA). Despite ambitious biodiversity commitments and a gradually expanding network of protected areas, many...
articles.body: EU marine protected areas: the challenge of turning the tide from paper to the sea in International Shipping News 27/10/2026 The EU’s marine protected areas often fail to receive effective protection, and the EU is unlikely to meet its 2030 marine conservation targets, according to a new report by the European Court of Auditors (ECA). Despite ambitious biodiversity commitments and a gradually expanding network of protected areas, many sites lack adequate conservation measures and climate adaptation planning, and report problems with staff and funding. Stakeholder involvement has become more inclusive but remains inconsistent, thus further limiting the effectiveness and long-term sustainability of marine conservation efforts. “The EU has made some progress in designating marine protected areas, but our audit shows that the true challenge is turning designation into actual protection. Turning political ambition into tangible results for marine ecosystems will require faster action, applicable protective measures, and a more coherent network across the EU’s seas,” said Iliana Ivanova, the ECA Member in charge of the audit. “To ensure that marine protected areas function effectively, we need the European Commission and member states to join forces, as well as engagement with local stakeholders.” The auditors warn that the EU is unlikely to meet its 2030 target of protecting 30 % of marine waters, with strict protection for 10 % of the total. Currently, around 14 % of EU marine waters are designated as protected, and less than 1 % as strictly protected. The auditors also found that the existing network is not working as a coherent ecological system, and that key offshore and deep-sea habitats are still inadequately protected. The fact is that designation as a marine protected area does not automatically lead to effective protection. The EU lacks a harmonised system of protection categories and corresponding activities compatible with its conservation objectives. For example, although fishing and other seabed-damaging activities pose a major threat to marine biodiversity, the auditors found that fishing restrictions apply to only a small share of protected areas. The auditors acknowledge the complexity of adopting conservation measures which affect fishing fleets from multiple member states. Nevertheless, they call for stronger cooperation at EU and national level to translate ‘marine protected area’ designations into harmonised, concrete and enforceable measures. This would also help to address funding challenges, since effective conservation requires substantial and predictable resources at a time when financing remains fragmented across national budgets and various EU instruments. The auditors warn that poor stakeholder involvement can weaken social sustainability, transparency, and public support for marine conservation measures, especially when coastal communities face significant socio-economic implications. Although member states are increasingly consulting stakeholders in more inclusive ways, they should give those who are affected more opportunities to contribute to decisions. Measures to mitigate the negative socio-economic effects of conservation measures should also be identified. The EU’s seas cover approximately 5 million km², an area larger than its landmass. About 40 % of the EU population lives within 50 km of a coast. The EU has four marine regions: the North-East Atlantic Ocean, the Mediterranean Sea, the Baltic Sea, and the Black Sea. These waters contain 3 648 Natura 2000 sites covering approximately 526 000 km², as well as 6 610 nationally-designated marine protected areas covering 244 000 km². More than half of the latter areas overlap with Natura 2000 sites. Special report 25/2026, “Marine protected areas – Designation alone is insufficient for meaningful protection”, is available on the ECA website, together with a one-page overview of its key facts and findings and an interactive dashboard presenting a map of EU marine protected areas. articles.body: Japan’s shipbuilders ramping up investment to double output in Shipbuilding News 27/10/2026 Japanese shipbuilders are stepping up capital investment in shipyards across the country as part of efforts to meet the government’s target of doubling domestic shipbuilding output, with the overall amount on track to exceed ¥1 trillion ($6.4 billion). A total of ¥900 billion in public- and private-sector investments have already been decided, including for the introduction of large cranes and the restoration of a dock damaged by an earthquake. Shipbuilders are eager to invest. At some shipyards, output is expected to more than double. Imabari Shipbuilding, Japan’s largest shipbuilder, plans to introduce jib cranes capable of lifting heavy loads and robots to increase steel plate-welding capacity at facilities including its headquarters in the city of Marugame, Kagawa Prefecture, and its Saijo Shipyard in the city of Saijo, Ehime Prefecture. The transport ministry has decided to provide ¥113.8 billion in subsidies to the Imabari Shipbuilding group through a fund for revitalizing the shipbuilding industry, the largest allocation yet. Total investments in the group are expected to reach around ¥300 billion. Imabari Shipbuilding said it will continually monitor production volumes as it works to double its output. Hakodate Dock, based in the city of Hakodate in Hokkaido, is moving to restore its No. 4 dock, which was rendered unusable by a major quake off southwestern Hokkaido in 1993. It plans to drain the dock to assess its condition before beginning restoration work, with shipbuilding there expected to resume around 2032. If the dock is restored, the company is expected to more than double its annual production of small bulk carriers from about five vessels in 2024. Together with investments at parent Namura Shipbuilding’s main shipyard in the city of Imari, Saga Prefecture, the two companies plan to invest up to about ¥150 billion over the next decade, including ¥49.9 billion in government aid. Kawasaki Heavy Industries, which is set to receive ¥15.6 billion in subsidies from the shipbuilding revitalization fund, plans to advance digitalization at its plant in the city of Sakaide, Kagawa Prefecture, including by introducing robots equipped with artificial intelligence. President Yasuhiko Hashimoto expressed determination to “transform shipbuilding sites” to address a shortage of workers such as skilled welders. Oshima Shipbuilding plans to install a crane and upgrade buildings at its Koyagi plant in Nagasaki, increasing its annual output of bulk carriers to about 10 vessels by around 2031, or 2.5 times the current level. As Japan’s shipbuilding industry has struggled to compete with rivals in China and South Korea, the government has designated it as one of 17 strategic fields for intensive investment. Japan aims to boost public- and private-sector investment in the industry to about ¥1 trillion by 2035 and double domestic shipbuilding output to 18 million gross tons from the 2024 level. However, the rising cost of production equipment such as cranes raises questions about whether investment plans will proceed as planned. “We greatly appreciate the government’s support, but our cash outflow is substantial,” an industry official said. “We need to scrutinize plans carefully.” Source: The Japan Times 2026-10-27 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: India seeks South Korean expertise to boost shipbuilding, targets global top five by 2047 in Shipbuilding News 27/10/2026 India is seeking South Korean expertise in shipbuilding, manufacturing and maritime technology as it works towards becoming one of the world’s top five shipbuilding nations by 2047, Union Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal said on October 25, as reported by PTI. Beginning a four-day visit to South Korea, Sonowal called on Indian professionals working in the country’s shipbuilding industry to help strengthen domestic shipyards, improve productivity and develop a skilled maritime workforce. The minister’s visit comes six months after India and South Korea adopted the VOYAGES framework to expand cooperation in shipbuilding, shipping and maritime logistics. India seeks Korean shipbuilding expertise Sonowal began his visit in Busan with an interaction involving Indian professionals associated with Samsung Heavy Industries, Hanwha Ocean, HD Hyundai, DNV and the Indian Register of Shipping. He urged them to use their experience in South Korea’s shipbuilding industry to support Indian companies, either by returning to India or working with them from overseas. “You can serve as living bridges between your networks in both countries,” Sonowal said, according to an official statement. The minister identified three priorities for cooperation: improving shipyard productivity and project execution, developing a globally competitive skilled workforce, and expanding partnerships in technology, manufacturing and innovation. India requires more shipbuilders, marine engineers, naval architects, designers, welders, project managers and technology specialists to support its maritime ambitions, he said. Sonowal also encouraged Indian professionals in Korea to mentor young workers and participate in initiatives such as the India Ship Technology Centre and a shipbuilding skills partnership involving the Korea International Cooperation Agency. India-South Korea shipbuilding partnership India and South Korea adopted the VOYAGES framework during South Korean President Lee Jae Myung’s state visit to India in April 2026. The framework seeks to connect South Korea’s shipbuilding capabilities with India’s plans to expand shipyards, maritime manufacturing and port infrastructure. One project under the partnership is a proposed mega shipyard at Thoothukudi in Tamil Nadu. An agreement signed in April between HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering, National Shipbuilding & Heavy Industries Park, Tamil Nadu, and Sagarmala Finance Corporation envisages a facility with an annual capacity of 2.5 million gross tonnes. The project is expected to generate approximately 15,000 direct jobs once operations stabilise, according to a government statement issued in May. At that time, preparation of its detailed project report was underway. The government’s Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047 aims to position India among the world’s five largest shipbuilding nations, with targeted annual shipbuilding output of 4.5 million gross tonnes. More industry meetings planned Sonowal is scheduled to meet shipbuilding industry leaders, maritime organisations and research institutions during his South Korea visit. “We are looking for partnership with Korea in shipbuilding, shipping, ports and maritime logistics,” he said. The minister is also scheduled to participate in a ministerial roundtable in Busan as part of the World Maritime Day Parallel Event on October 26. The discussions are expected to focus on international maritime cooperation and implementation of industry regulations. Source: Moneycontrol 2026-10-27 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Europe Offshore Eni locks in offshore contractors for Cyprus gas project Bojan Lepic October 27, 2026 0 98 1 minute read Eni Eni Italian energy major Eni has signed the main engineering, procurement, construction, and drilling contracts for the Cronos gas development offshore Cyprus, with a string of major offshore contractors securing work on the project. The contracts, valued by local media at around $1.8bn, mark the start of the development’s execution phase in Block 6, following a final investment decision by Eni and partner TotalEnergies in July. Although Eni did not disclose the contractors involved, local media identified eight companies awarded work on the development, covering subsea production systems, pipelines, offshore installation, drilling and associated infrastructure. Baker Hughes will design, procure, and construct subsea production systems, while TechnipFMC will supply flexible gas production lines. Dalmine has been selected to supply gas export and monoethylene glycol pipelines, with Oceaneering International responsible for subsea umbilicals and control systems. China Merchants Heavy Industry will design, construct, transport, and install a floating control unit. US offshore engineering contractor McDermott will handle offshore transportation, installation, tie-ins, and commissioning of subsea pipelines and equipment. McDermott had already announced a contract worth between $500m and $750m for Cronos in September, marking its first subsea project award from Eni. Egyptian contractor Petrojet will construct a new onshore gas pipeline connecting the Zohr facilities with the Damietta LNG terminal, while Italy’s Saipem has been selected to provide drilling services using its Saipem 10000 drillship. Separately, Halliburton secured a bundled well construction and completions contract for Cronos in September, covering drilling fluids, directional drilling, cementing, automation, and other well services. The Cronos development will involve four subsea wells targeting resources estimated at more than 3trn cubic feet of gas initially in place. Production is expected to begin in the first half of 2028, reaching a plateau of up to 500m standard cubic feet per day. Gas will be transported to Egypt for processing through existing Zohr-field infrastructure before being liquefied at Damietta for export, primarily to European markets. Eni operates Block 6 with a 50% stake, while TotalEnergies holds the remaining interest. articles.title: Container freight rates diverge as global benchmarks rise and Asian indexes weaken
articles.summary: Global container freight rates delivered a mixed performance in the latest weekly assessments, with major international benchmarks moving higher while Chinese freight indexes showed more subdued results. The divergence was particularly evident on Asia-Europe routes, where Drewry reported further increases but the...
articles.body: Global container freight rates delivered a mixed performance in the latest weekly assessments, with major international benchmarks moving higher while Chinese freight indexes showed more subdued results. The divergence was particularly evident on Asia-Europe routes, where Drewry reported further increases but the NYSHEX Freight Index (NYFI) continued to decline. Drewry’s World Container Index (WCI) rose 2% to US$4,585 per 40-foot container, reaching its highest level in 15 weeks. The Freightos Baltic Index (FBX) also advanced, increasing 5% to US$3,560. Meanwhile, the China Containerized Freight Index (CCFI) declined, while the Shanghai Containerized Freight Index (SCFI) and Ningbo Containerized Freight Index (NCFI) registered marginal gains. The latest figures highlight an uneven freight market, with movements varying considerably across benchmarks and individual trade lanes. Chinese freight indexes show limited momentum The SCFI edged up 0.05% to 3,681.34 points on 23 October, compared with 3,679.58 in the previous assessment. The marginal increase indicates broadly stable conditions in the index. The CCFI moved in the opposite direction, declining approximately 2.41% to 1,876.27 points from 1,922.64 a week earlier. It was the most pronounced movement among the three Chinese composite indexes. The NCFI increased approximately 0.50% to 2,509.30 points, compared with 2,496.79 in the preceding assessment. Together, these readings present a mixed picture. While SCFI and NCFI remained in positive territory, their gains were considerably smaller than those recorded by the FBX and Drewry WCI. NYFI records further Asia-Europe weakness The NYFI assessment published on 23 October showed contrasting developments across the five monitored trade lanes. On the Transpacific, Asia-US West Coast increased 1.39% to 7,579.09, compared with 7,475.40 a week earlier. Asia-US East Coast remained virtually unchanged, declining 0.02% to 9,936.89 from 9,938.75. The figures indicate relatively stable Transpacific conditions, with modest improvement on the West Coast and little movement on the East Coast. Asia-North Europe continued to weaken, declining 2.53% to 3,039.67 from 3,118.71. The latest decrease followed a 7.08% decline in the previous assessment, extending the downward movement on the route. The Transatlantic market recorded sharper declines. Westbound rates fell 7.30% to 2,882.09 from 3,109.16, partially reversing the previous week’s 14.77% increase. Eastbound rates experienced an even steeper reduction, dropping 19.28% to 946.64 from 1,172.79. This followed an 8.53% decrease in the preceding assessment. The two Transatlantic movements were among the most significant developments in the latest NYFI readings, illustrating substantial week-to-week volatility. Drewry WCI reaches a 15-week high Drewry’s WCI increased 2% to US$4,585 per 40-foot container on 22 October, marking its second consecutive weekly increase and highest level in 15 weeks. On the Transpacific, Shanghai-Los Angeles rose 2% to US$8,007 per 40-foot container, while Shanghai-New York increased 1% to US$10,166. Asia-Europe routes also recorded further gains. Shanghai-Rotterdam increased 3% to US$3,632, while Shanghai-Genoa climbed 5% to US$4,152. According to Drewry, carriers have announced eight blank sailings on Asia-Europe services for the following week, compared with two in the current week. The consultancy linked the increase in cancelled sailings to efforts to manage available capacity and support freight rates. On the Transpacific, announced blank sailings declined from six to two. Drewry expects rates on these routes to remain broadly stable, while anticipating a slight increase on Asia-Europe. These expectations remain forecasts rather than confirmed future market movements. FBX Global Index posts stronger growth The FBX Global Container Freight Index increased 5% to US$3,560, compared with approximately US$3,397 in the previous weekly reading. The increase was stronger than the 2% advance recorded in the preceding assessment, indicating continued upward movement in the global benchmark. The FBX and WCI therefore both recorded gains for a second consecutive week, although their respective increases differed. Their positive performance contrasts with the decline in the CCFI and the limited changes recorded by the SCFI and NCFI. Asia-Europe remains the main point of divergence One of the clearest differences in the latest assessments concerns Asia-Europe freight rates. Drewry reported increases of 3% on Shanghai-Rotterdam and 5% on Shanghai-Genoa, extending the recovery recorded in its previous assessment. In contrast, NYFI Asia-North Europe declined 2.53%, following a substantially larger decrease a week earlier. The difference is important but should not be interpreted as a direct contradiction. NYFI and Drewry apply different methodologies and reporting periods, while their route definitions and underlying rate assessments are not identical. The NYFI is based on reported transactions involving containers that have actually shipped, whereas Drewry’s WCI provides assessed spot freight rate benchmarks. Consequently, the two indexes can report different short-term movements within related markets. Market outlook The latest assessments suggest that the recovery in global container freight benchmarks has continued, but its strength varies considerably across the market. Drewry’s WCI and the FBX recorded further increases, supported by stronger readings on several major East-West routes. However, the decline in the CCFI and the limited gains in the SCFI and NCFI indicate that the improvement is not uniform across Chinese freight benchmarks. Asia-Europe remains a key area to monitor, particularly as Drewry anticipates tighter capacity following an increase in announced blank sailings. On the Transpacific, NYFI and Drewry point to broadly stable or moderately firmer conditions, although the extent of improvement differs between routes. Meanwhile, the sharp declines in both Transatlantic directions reported by NYFI underline the volatility affecting individual markets. The next weekly assessments will provide a clearer indication of whether the recent increases in global benchmarks can be sustained and whether the differing Asia-Europe readings begin to converge.
takeaways: Global container freight rates delivered a mixed performance in the latest weekly assessments, with major international benchmarks moving higher while Chinese freight indexes showed more subdued results.
The divergence was particularly evident on Asia-Europe routes, where Drewry reported further increases but the NYSHEX Freight Index (NYFI) continued to decline.
Drewry’s World Container Index (WCI) rose 2% to US$4,585 per 40-foot container, reaching its highest level in 15 weeks.

articles.body: Middle East Operations Asyad Group prices $132m shipping stake sale Adis Ajdin October 27, 2026 0 149 1 minute read Asyad Shipping Asyad Shipping Oman’s Asyad Group has priced an institutional share sale in its listed shipping subsidiary at OMR50.8m ($132m), reducing its ownership as part of a move to broaden the company’s shareholder base. Muscat-listed Asyad Shipping said the institutional bookbuilding process closed heavily oversubscribed. The transaction covers 5% of Asyad Shipping’s issued share capital. The transaction follows Asyad Shipping’s March 2025 initial public offering, which raised approximately $333m and brought 20% of the company into public ownership. Since listing, the company has continued expanding and renewing its fleet across the tanker, dry bulk, gas and container sectors. Asyad operated a fleet of 91 vessels at the end of June, including 48 owned or co-owned ships, 31 chartered-in vessels and 12 newbuildings. Its latest investment programme includes eight charter-backed MR product tankers ordered at HD Hyundai and three VLCCs contracted at Hanwha Ocean earlier this year. The company has also been recycling capital through secondhand sales. In September, it agreed to dispose of three ageing tankers for a combined OMR68.44m ($178m), including two VLCCs. articles.title: Dolphin Drilling parts ways with 52-year-old rig and forges pact with SPM
articles.summary: Dolphin Drilling has sealed a deal to divest its 1974-built rig for up to $25 million and formed a strategic partnership with SPM.
articles.body: Business & Finance October 27, 2026 · 7 hours ago Dolphin Drilling parts ways with 52-year-old rig and forges pact with SPM Dolphin Drilling has sealed a deal to divest its 1974-built rig for up to $25 million and formed a strategic partnership with SPM. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 4 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Blackford Dolphin rig; Source: Dolphin Drilling Dolphin Drilling, an Oslo-listed, Aberdeen-headquartered owner and operator of a fleet of harsh-environment mid-water and deepwater semi-submersible drilling rigs, has taken a step to strengthen its financial position, offloading its semi-submersible rig for $25 million in a transaction expected to close next month in Singapore, while partnering with SPM Energy Shipping FZCO to capture upside in a tightening global rig market. Dolphin Drilling has entered into a definitive sale and purchase agreement (SPA) for the sale of the 1974-built Blackford Dolphin semi-submersible rig with SPM for a total consideration of $25 million, comprising $10 million, payable upon delivery of the rig and $15 million, payable when SPM receives the first payment under a potential future drilling contract. The sale is expected to close on or about November 5, 2026, in Singapore, immediately and materially reducing the firm’s operating cost base, eliminating the class renewal survey capital expenditures related to this rig and significantly strengthening the company’s financial position. The duo has also entered into a memorandum of understanding (MoU) for the management of future drilling contracts for this rig and one additional semi-submersible, as well as any other rigs or units that the two companies may agree upon. The company explains that these management arrangements contemplate entry into management agreements and other deals, which remain subject to definitive documentation and customary closing conditions. The contemplated management arrangements combine Dolphin Drilling’s established operating platform, technical expertise and long track record with the strong commercial presence of the participating companies in India and the surrounding regions. The rigs will be marketed by SPM in India and other areas agreed upon between the two players, with capital costs, operational expenses and guarantees related to future drilling contracts to be covered by SPM as owners of the rigs. Ronny Bjørnådal , Chairman of the Board of Directors of Dolphin Drilling, commented: “Dolphin Drilling will through the sale and contemplated management arrangements materially de-risk the company and at the same time, significantly reduce operating costs as well as eliminate capital expenditures associated with the class renewal survey for the Blackford Dolphin. “The transactions provide for potential future upside through management of Blackford Dolphin and one or more additional semi-submersible drilling rig resulting in future management fees and ability to grow our platform.” Related Articles Fossil Energy Dolphin Drilling: GHL cash-and-rig proposal ‘encouraging’ but settlement offer falls short 2 min read Dolphin Drilling believes the sale and management arrangements offer a compelling combination of immediate risk reduction and value realization while preserving exposure to the potential upside from improving offshore drilling market fundamentals and a further tightening of the supply and demand balance. The transactions are highly attractive to the company, as they are expected to reduce the company’s interest-bearing debt and its capital expenditures related to Blackford Dolphin while creating opportunities for future revenue generation from the semi-submersible and other rigs under management, complementing the firm’s existing operating model with capital-light revenue streams. Bjørnådal emphasized: “The management arrangements would combine SPM’s commercial capabilities, market access and relationships in some of the most active benign-water markets in the world with Dolphin Drilling’s established operating platform, technical expertise and worldwide operating licenses, a proven operating platform and decades of experience. “This gives us the flexibility to capture the prospective upside of a tightening rig market, while strengthening our platform and driving long-term shareholder value.” The strategic partnership aligns well with Dolphin Drilling’s broader, ongoing evaluation of strategic initiatives and business opportunities to participate in industry consolidation and further growth. The company reported at the end of second quarter 2026 improved financial figures, including total cash of $55.1 million and a firm revenue contracted backlog of $556 million, with a further $446 million in options, resulting from multi-year contracts secured for Paul B. articles.body: FedEx Corporation has appointed Jamere Jackson as its new Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, effective November 30, 2026. Jackson will succeed Claude Russ, who has served as interim CFO since June 1. The appointment brings an experienced financial executive to the global transportation and logistics company. Jackson joins FedEx from AutoZone, where he has served as Chief Financial Officer since January 2021. Most recently, he also oversaw the company’s Finance and Store Development functions. Before joining AutoZone, Jackson held senior financial leadership positions at several major companies. These included Hertz Global Holdings and Nielsen Holdings, where he served as CFO. Earlier in his career, he also held various leadership roles at General Electric. His responsibilities included serving as CFO of a division within GE Oil and Gas. In addition, Jackson serves on the Board of Directors of Eli Lilly & Co., where he chairs the Audit Committee. FedEx focuses on financial performance and growth FedEx President and CEO Raj Subramaniam welcomed Jackson to the company’s executive leadership team. “I am pleased to welcome Jamere to FedEx and the executive leadership team,” said Raj Subramaniam, President and CEO of FedEx Corporation. Subramaniam highlighted Jackson’s experience in financial management, capital allocation and operational performance. He also expressed confidence that the appointment would support FedEx’s strategy for profitable growth. The FedEx CEO thanked Claude Russ for his leadership during the interim period and his contributions to the company. Meanwhile, Jackson expressed enthusiasm about joining the logistics group and working with its financial leadership team. “FedEx is a remarkable business with an extraordinary team and significant opportunity ahead,” Jackson said. He added that he looks forward to supporting the company’s profitable growth strategy and applying his previous financial leadership experience. The appointment will take effect on November 30, completing the transition from the company’s interim financial leadership arrangements.

articles.title: What cargo shipping can learn from cruise about crewing technology
articles.summary: Raal Harris, the founder of PitchFrame, brings readers details of an interesting session from last week’s Crew Connect Global in Manila. We spend a lot of time in cargo shipping looking to aviation for inspiration in approaches to safety, technology, training and operational efficiency. But there’s another industry...
articles.body: Contributions Operations Tech What cargo shipping can learn from cruise about crewing technology Splash October 27, 2026 0 266 7 minutes read Associated British Ports Associated British Ports Raal Harris, the founder of PitchFrame, brings readers details of an interesting session from last week’s Crew Connect Global in Manila. We spend a lot of time in cargo shipping looking to aviation for inspiration in approaches to safety, technology, training and operational efficiency. But there’s another industry sitting much closer to home that perhaps deserves more of our attention: cruise. At Crew Connect Global in Manila, I had the opportunity to explore this theme with four people who understand the cruise sector from very different perspectives: Eric Visser of Holland America Line and Seabourn, Anca Preda of Columbia Shipmanagement, Calypso Diareme of ATPI and Joost van Ree of Nevetal. Our question was straightforward: what can cargo shipping actually learn from the way cruise manages its crew, and particularly from the technology that supports it? The discussion revealed some important differences, but also some surprisingly transferable lessons. And while cruise may be further ahead in certain aspects of crew management technology, the most interesting differences aren’t necessarily the systems themselves. They’re what those systems enable organisations to do. Different scale, different challenges We should start by acknowledging that cruise and cargo operate under very different conditions. Eric Visser explained that Holland America Line and Seabourn employ around 16,000 people across their fleet, with between 10 and 40 crew joining or leaving individual vessels almost every day. A large cruise ship might carry 1,000 or even 2,000 crew, compared with perhaps 20 to 25 on a typical cargo vessel. Then there’s predictability. Cruise operators can know 18 to 24 months in advance where their ships will be, often down to the hour. That makes workforce planning, crew changes and training considerably easier to organise than in cargo shipping, where schedules and port calls are subject to disruption at a moment’s notice. But scale and predictability aren’t the only differences. Cruise ships have entire departments dedicated to HR, training and employee welfare. They manage complex workforces covering everything from navigation and engineering to hospitality, entertainment and catering. And the people working in those departments are directly responsible for delivering the product that customers have paid for. As Eric memorably put it, “Our cargo talks back to us.” A passenger’s experience is shaped by the people they encounter, and poor performance can translate almost immediately into customer dissatisfaction and reputational damage that impacts the bottom line. That creates a very visible commercial incentive to invest in the workforce. Cargo shipping has equally important dependencies on the competence, wellbeing and performance of its seafarers, but the relationship with commercial performance is often less immediate and less visible. This distinction helps explain why cruise has developed some of its approaches to crew management. It also raises the first important question for cargo: are we giving our people the strategic attention their contribution deserves? Building a workforce, not just filling vacancies One of the most interesting distinctions Eric made concerned the relationship between ship operators and the organisations that supply their crew. In his organisation, they don’t refer to manning agents. They call them talent partners. That might sound like a cosmetic change, but the thinking behind it is significant. A traditional crewing transaction starts with a vacancy. The operator needs a third engineer, the agency identifies a qualified candidate, and that person joins the ship. In cruise, Eric described a much more continuous relationship, where the recruitment partner shares responsibility for supporting the seafarer throughout their employment, including their wellbeing, development and career progression. “We’re really building a workforce rather than that we are building a portfolio of people,” he explained. The distinction is important. One approach is principally concerned with meeting today’s crewing requirements. The other is concerned with developing the people and capabilities the organisation will need tomorrow. Anca Preda reinforced this point, explaining that cruise has developed a much broader maritime HR function, with greater emphasis on employee engagement, employer branding, talent development and retention. “We don’t look at talent attraction as an administrative function,” she told us. Of course, a cargo vessel cannot accommodate a dedicated onboard HR department. But Anca argued that this needn’t prevent cargo operators from adopting the underlying approach. These responsibilities can be managed from shore, provided the organisation establishes the right relationships, processes and accountability. This is perhaps the first genuinely transferable lesson. Strategic workforce management doesn’t depend on having thousands of employees on a vessel. It depends on recognising that recruitment, development, deployment and retention are connected activities rather than separate administrative tasks. What the data tells us about people Of course planning and coordination at this scale require technology and data that can support a more strategic approach. Eric offered an excellent example. His organisation had experienced turnover of around 30% within one group of officers. The natural assumption was that remuneration was the problem. But when they examined the available workforce information, they discovered that the more significant issue was a bottleneck in career progression. People couldn’t see a route to promotion. Addressing that problem reduced turnover. It’s a simple example, but an important one. Without the data, the organisation might have responded by increasing pay, potentially at considerable expense, without resolving the underlying issue. Cruise operators are increasingly connecting information about recruitment, competence, training, career progression, deployment and retention to build a more complete picture of their workforce. This also creates opportunities to take a more sophisticated approach to professional development. Eric described how cross-training allows people to move between departments and progress through different roles. Rather than viewing an individual solely in terms of the job they currently perform, the organisation considers their existing competencies, their potential and the additional development needed to prepare them for another role. Anca described exploring how AI might automate part of this process, comparing role requirements, identifying competency gaps and suggesting the training needed to support career progression. That is a much more interesting application of AI than simply making existing administrative processes faster. It could help organisations understand not only whether they have enough people, but whether they are developing the right capabilities for future requirements. There is, however, an important prerequisite. Joost van Ree pointed out that some cruise operators already have relatively mature data platforms, developed initially to support commercial functions such as reservations, finance and customer satisfaction. Connecting crew management, learning and other operational systems to those platforms creates opportunities for more predictive workforce planning. Cargo shipping, by contrast, often still relies heavily on spreadsheets, PDFs and disconnected systems. The challenge isn’t necessarily a lack of data. It’s the inability to bring that information together into something sufficiently reliable to support decisions. And that matters even more as organisations begin to introduce AI. Predictive systems are only as useful as the information on which they depend. When planning meets reality Perhaps the most striking operational example came from Calypso Diareme, who works across both cruise and cargo crew logistics at ATPI. She described the challenges of managing crew movements during the recent Middle East crisis. ATPI had to arrange the evacuation of several thousand cruise crew, alongside much smaller numbers of cargo seafarers requiring changes to their travel arrangements. According to Calypso, the cruise movements were completed within days, while some of the cargo movements took weeks. The difference wasn’t simply the availability of technology. Cruise operators had developed processes following COVID that allowed the various parties involved to work from connected information. They knew who needed to travel, what documentation those individuals held, which routes were available, who needed to be involved and what alternatives existed when plans changed. In cargo, individual crew changes were more likely to be treated as separate cases, requiring people to gather information and coordinate arrangements afresh. This is a particularly useful illustration of what digital maturity actually means. A crew-change platform might optimise a travel itinerary, but that is of limited value if the crewing department, travel provider, port agent and vessel are working from different information. Similarly, an algorithm might identify the ideal person for an assignment, but that doesn’t help much if the person cannot reach the ship. The value comes from connecting the whole process, from workforce planning through to successful embarkation, and ensuring that people can respond effectively when something goes wrong. Technology enables that coordination, but it cannot substitute for the processes, relationships and human judgement needed to make it work. For cargo operators, where crew changes are often less predictable, that capability may be particularly valuable. Don’t copy cruise. Learn from it. There is a temptation, when looking at a more technologically mature operation, to assume that the answer is to acquire the same systems, but that is not necessarily the case. Cruise operators have scale, operational characteristics and commercial incentives that can justify investments which would make little sense for many cargo fleets. And cruise itself isn’t a single model. Expedition vessels, river cruise operators and smaller luxury ships face different challenges from the largest ocean-going cruise vessels. Joost’s closing advice was particularly sensible: “Don’t overspend chasing cruise-level solutions.” The opportunity is to adopt the principles that make those solutions effective, rather than replicate their complexity. That might mean connecting existing workforce data before investing in new AI applications. It might mean developing a clearer understanding of competency and promotion readiness rather than simply tracking training completion. Or it might mean redesigning crew-change processes so that information can move reliably between the organisations involved. It also means giving maritime HR a stronger voice in operational and commercial decision-making. As Eric argued, HR should be regarded as a strategic partner in the development of the business, not simply the function responsible for supplying people. None of this requires cargo shipping to become more like cruise in its wider operating model. It requires us to think differently about how we use technology to manage, support and develop the people on whom our operations depend. My biggest takeaway from the discussion was that cruise’s advantage isn’t simply that it has more sophisticated technology. In many cases, it has developed a more connected approach to workforce management, supported by better information, clearer processes and a stronger understanding of the commercial value of its people. And that is something cargo shipping can learn from, regardless of fleet size. articles.title: GXO and Agility Robotics expand humanoid robot deployment across US warehouses
articles.summary: GXO Logistics and Agility Robotics have announced plans to expand their partnership by deploying humanoid robots at two additional logistics facilities in the United States. The expansion will bring Agility Robotics’ Digit robots to GXO warehouses in Statesville, North Carolina, and Lebanon, Tennessee. Deployments...
articles.body: GXO Logistics and Agility Robotics have announced plans to expand their partnership by deploying humanoid robots at two additional logistics facilities in the United States. The expansion will bring Agility Robotics’ Digit robots to GXO warehouses in Statesville, North Carolina, and Lebanon, Tennessee. Deployments are expected to begin in early 2027, supporting e-commerce fulfillment and repetitive material-handling tasks. The announcement, made on October 26, builds on the companies’ existing commercial partnership. Their collaboration has already demonstrated the use of humanoid robots in active warehouse operations. At GXO’s Flowery Branch facility in Georgia, Digit robots have moved more than 100,000 totes since their initial deployment. The robots work alongside existing warehouse automation, transferring containers and placing them onto conveyor systems. The latest agreement marks a further step towards expanding humanoid robotics beyond a single operating site. GXO expands commercial use of humanoid robots GXO and Agility Robotics began collaborating in late 2023 through a proof-of-concept project at the Flowery Branch warehouse. In June 2024, the companies signed a multi-year Robots-as-a-Service (RaaS) agreement. This introduced Digit robots into live warehouse operations under a commercial arrangement. The deployment also included Agility Arc, a cloud-based platform designed to manage robot fleets and integrate them with warehouse systems. Since then, the companies have continued developing the technology through practical operational experience. “Innovation is most powerful when it delivers practical solutions that create value for our customers and our people,” said Patrick Kelleher, CEO of GXO. Kelleher explained that the partnership has focused on turning emerging technology into operational improvements. He also highlighted the potential of humanoid robots to support employees and customers. The next phase will introduce Digit 4 robots at the two additional GXO facilities. The companies then plan to transition to Digit 5 once the newer model becomes commercially available. Digit 5, unveiled in September 2026, is designed to operate safely alongside people and perform a wider range of industrial tasks. Agility Robotics prepares for wider commercial deployment The expansion comes as Agility Robotics increases its efforts to support larger commercial deployments. Across its commercial operations and customer programmes, Digit has accumulated more than 65,000 hours of real-world operation. According to the company, this experience has helped shape the development of its next-generation robots. “GXO was the first customer to put Digit to work in live operations under a commercial agreement, and expanding to additional sites is the clearest signal that the value is real,” said Peggy Johnson, CEO of Agility Robotics. Johnson added that customers are increasingly focusing on where humanoid robots can be deployed at scale rather than whether the technology can operate in warehouses. To support future growth, Agility has developed RoboFab, a manufacturing facility in Salem, Oregon. The 70,000-square-foot site is designed for an annual production capacity of up to 10,000 robots. The company is also expanding its software, deployment and support capabilities. These investments aim to support the wider adoption of humanoid robotics across industrial and logistics operations. Meanwhile, Agility is preparing to become a publicly traded company through a proposed business combination with Churchill Capital Corp XI. The transaction is expected to close during the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to completion. Following the proposed combination, Agility Robotics is expected to trade on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol AGLT. For GXO, the latest expansion reflects its strategy of introducing advanced automation into existing warehouse operations. The companies have not disclosed the number of robots planned for the new facilities or the financial value of the expanded agreement. However, the move from one operating warehouse to multiple sites represents a further stage in the commercial deployment of humanoid robots within the logistics industry.
